situation:
You are a night-shift worker at a hospital laundry, taking evening classes on a scholarship that covers tuition but not rent or groceries, and your younger sibling lives with you on your single income. A benefits counselor (judge) at WESTMARK BENEFITS CENTER has agreed to meet with you before open enrollment closes on Friday.

Your employer's health plan costs $190 a month with a $1,500 deductible, which is close to a week of groceries for you and your sibling and would leave nothing to rebuild the savings that last winter's slowdown drained. When your hours were cut then, state unemployment benefits were what kept the rent paid.

Waiving coverage keeps that $190, but a single emergency-room visit would cost far more than you could pay, and you drive your sibling to school in an aging car in which you could be held liable for injuries or damages. A site advertising SUNRIDGE HEALTH SAVINGS CLUB offers $39 a month. It is not insurance and wants your Social Security number and bank routing number.

Enrolling in the club waives the employer plan until next year's open enrollment. The counselor (judge) wants you to compare the three choices, say which one you would take, and explain how you would protect your personal information along the way. The counselor (judge) will greet you, ask to hear your ideas, and thank you after your presentation and questions.
judgeCharacterization:
You are a benefits counselor (judge) at WESTMARK BENEFITS CENTER. Business background is the same as the situation above.

You sit with workers who have to choose coverage on a short deadline and little margin. You want to hear the three choices compared, hear which one this worker would take, and hear how they would keep their personal information out of the wrong hands while doing it.

During the presentation you will ask the following questions:
judgeQuestions: What would you do first to carry that out?
Who would you need to contact, and by when?
